source.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine Translation
source.authors: A. Bau; Yonatan Belinkov; Hassan Sajjad; Nadir Durrani; Fahim Dalvi; James R. Glass

record.tranche_reason: The study compares representations from independently trained NMT models using neuron correlations, regression and SVCCA, then tests whether highly ranked neurons matter. This is a different measurement and setting from the original convergence work.
record.gate_note: The study directly measures cross-model neuron correlations and reports recurring linguistic properties, so these results bear on shared features. The erasure experiments test the importance of neurons selected by those cross-model methods. Translation-control results deliberately induced by changing activations are not evidence of naturally occurring convergence and are left out. Model-quality and linguistic-prediction results not tied to cross-model sharing are also left out.
record.test_reason: Convergence is mainly the paper's ranking tool, but it reports cross-model results in a new setting: 500-d LSTM NMT encoders trained on different data and target languages. Table 2 finds a parentheses neuron in each of 15 models, and Table 3 gives cross-model correlations with a tense neuron. Both bear on V5. Erasure results only validate the paper's own ranking method.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that cross-model-shared neurons matter far more to translation quality than unshared ones. They add that many individual neurons capture interpretable properties (position, parentheses, tense, noun phrases), and that tense, number and gender can be partly controlled by editing neurons (67%, 37%, 21% best success). Cross-model similarity is their working hypothesis and tool rather than the main object of study. They attribute the lower tense alignment in the auto-encoder to the copying objective, and in Chinese to the lack of tense marking.
record.recipe_differences: Uses neuron-level correlations, linear regression and SVCCA to find shared information in recurrent NMT models, then erases selected neurons to check translation impact. It does not reproduce the original convergence method.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports differences among correlation-based rankings and SVCCA; correlations for tense are lower in English-Chinese models and English auto-encoders.

fits_no_version.finding: Erasing neurons ranked high by cross-model correlation (MaxCorr/MinCorr/LinReg) costs 15-20 BLEU at 10%, vs 2-3 BLEU for the bottom 10%. Erasing the top 1% of SVCCA directions costs 15 BLEU.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Features shared across independently trained models are functionally more important to each model than unshared ones.

record.problems: No model scale or capability comparison; the tested systems are 500-dimensional LSTMs trained on UN data. Table 3 does not assign correlation values to specific checkpoints. Some cross-language erasure results are described qualitatively or shown in figures, and no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Translation-control interventions in Section 6 and Table 4 were deliberately induced by modifying activations, so they do not test naturally occurring convergence. Other linguistic-property probes, token/position variance results, and additional catalog entries are not separate evidence of cross-model convergence for the versions tested here.

untested.parts: No scale or capability variation; all models are 500-d 2-layer LSTMs.
Models differ in training data subset and target language; no pure seed comparison. Unit-level vs subspace sharing across seeds is not separated.
LinReg and SVCCA are used only to rank neurons; no mapping, stitching or transfer performance is reported.
Ranking methods find different neuron types (position vs token identity), but convergence is not tested for dependence on measure settings or input distribution.
No plateau analysis. Only an incidental hint that objective matters: the auto-encoder shows lower tense correlation.

missing.what: Text says all neurons most correlated with the tense neuron rank in the top 5 for tense F1, and 9 of 15 are their model's best tense predictor. This is direct evidence the correlated neurons encode the same feature.

record.verdict_notes: V3 links were removed because models vary in training data and target language, not only initialization. Noun-phrase neurons found in every network (60-80% accuracy, Table 5) would also support V5, but rows_left_out declares them. Section 6 control results are correctly excluded as deliberately induced.

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep, and no measurement of representation alignment as models get larger or more capable.
No vision-language models or paired image-caption representations.
Models are not explicitly compared across random initializations; the study varies training data and language pairs. It does not establish that individual units or bases are the same.

The study uses correlation, regression and SVCCA to rank neurons or directions, but does not report representation-transfer or stitching performance, or show that one model can substitute for another.
The study examines recurring linguistic properties in NMT neurons, not recurrence of specific circuits or SAE features.
It compares neuron-ranking methods, but does not test whether a convergence result depends on similarity settings or input distributions.
No test of whether alignment plateaus or is explained by shared training data or objectives rather than a common model of reality.

relationships.condition: NMT encoders (en→es/fr/ar/ru/zh); parentheses and tense features
relationships.reason: In 13 of 15 models a distinct parentheses neuron (F1 0.54-0.76, far above the 2nd-best) is found and usually ranked high by MaxCorr (r1-r5, r8-r15). The tense neuron has cross-model correlates of |0.50-0.69| in NMT models (r16-r19).
relationships.display_finding: Distinct parentheses neurons appeared in 13 of 15 models with F1 scores of 0.54–0.76, usually ranking highly by MaxCorr, while tense neurons had cross-model absolute correlations of 0.50–0.69.

relation.reason: Tables 2 and 3 directly measure recurring interpretable neurons; the paper also tests the importance of shared information through erasure.

tranche.reason: Extends cross-model neuron comparison to recurrent NMT encoders and reports shared interpretable features across training datasets and target languages.

source_check.notes: Table 3 reports signed correlations for neurons selected by absolute correlation; negative signs indicate polarity. Models share an architecture but differ in training data and target language/objective, so these results do not isolate convergence across seeds.

statements.correction: Table 2: en-es-2:208 top-neuron F1 0.72; second-best-neuron F1 0.26. Section 4: UN corpus; 500-dimensional, two-layer LSTM models. Sections 5.1 and 5.3: erasure controls and recurring interpretable neurons. Peer-review status: not established by supplied text.
statements.problem: The NMT empirical claims are supported; the supplied arXiv text does not establish the asserted peer-review status.
